```{r}
pca_recipe <- recipe(school ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  update_role(case, new_role = "ID") |>
  step_zv(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 5, keep_original_cols = TRUE) |>
  prep()

pca_data <- pca_recipe |>
  bake(train_data) |>
  select(case, PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4, PC5, school, everything())

pca_fit <- pca_recipe$steps[[3]]$res
eigenvalues <- pca_fit |> tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")
n_tests <- sum(str_starts(names(train_data), "t"))
ev <- function(k, what = "percent") eigenvalues[[what]][k]
```

```{r}
#| label: visuals
#| include: false
# ---- Why reduce: distances stop telling points apart as variables are added
set.seed(1)
curse <- map_dfr(c(1, 2, 5, 10, 24, 100, 1000), function(d) {
  X <- matrix(runif(200 * d), ncol = d)
  D <- as.matrix(dist(X)); diag(D) <- NA
  tibble(d = d, ratio = median(apply(D, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE) / apply(D, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)))
})
curse_at <- function(d) curse$ratio[curse$d == d]
set.seed(4)
cust <- tibble(income = runif(30, 15, 95), debt = runif(30, 0, 60))
me <- cust[7, ]
cust <- cust |> mutate(d1 = abs(income - me$income), d2 = sqrt((income - me$income)^2 + (debt - me$debt)^2))
curse_step <- function(k) {
  if (k == 1) {
    ggplot(cust, aes(income, 0)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = grey) +
      geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.6, colour = grey) +
      geom_point(data = filter(cust, d1 < 6), size = 4, colour = red) +
      geom_point(data = me, size = 6, shape = 23, fill = "white", colour = navy, stroke = 1.8) +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = NULL) +
      theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
      labs(x = "Income (£k)", y = NULL,
           title = paste0("Who is similar to the diamond? ", sum(cust$d1 < 6) - 1, " customers within £6k"))
  } else if (k == 2) {
    circ <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200), income = me$income + 6 * cos(t), debt = me$debt + 6 * sin(t))
    ggplot(cust, aes(income, debt)) +
      geom_path(data = circ, colour = navy, linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.6, colour = grey) +
      geom_point(data = filter(cust, d2 < 6), size = 4, colour = red) +
      geom_point(data = me, size = 6, shape = 23, fill = "white", colour = navy, stroke = 1.8) +
      coord_fixed() + theme_slide() +
      labs(x = "Income (£k)", y = "Debt (£k)",
           title = paste0("Two variables: ", sum(cust$d2 < 6) - 1, " within the same distance"))
  } else {
    ggplot(curse, aes(d, ratio)) +
      geom_line(colour = red, linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(colour = red, size = 3.5) +
      geom_point(data = filter(curse, d == 24), colour = navy, size = 6, shape = 21, stroke = 1.6) +
      annotate("text", x = 24, y = curse_at(24) * 3.2, label = "24 variables:\ntoday's data", colour = navy, size = 4.6, lineheight = 0.9) +
      scale_x_log10(breaks = curse$d, labels = big(curse$d)) + scale_y_log10() +
      theme_slide() +
      labs(x = "Number of variables", y = "Farthest ÷ nearest neighbour",
           title = "Many variables: everyone is about equally far")
  }
}

# ---- PCA intuition: the school report. Forty made-up pupils, a maths and a physics mark.
set.seed(3)
ability <- rnorm(40)
report <- tibble(maths = 60 + 11 * ability + rnorm(40, 0, 4.5), physics = 58 + 11 * ability + rnorm(40, 0, 4.5))
rp <- prcomp(report)
if (sum(rp$rotation[, 1]) < 0) rp$rotation[, 1] <- -rp$rotation[, 1]
rp_var <- rp$sdev^2 / sum(rp$sdev^2)
ctr <- rp$center; v1 <- rp$rotation[, 1]; v2 <- rp$rotation[, 2]
sc <- sweep(as.matrix(report), 2, ctr) %*% rp$rotation
report <- report |> mutate(pc1 = sc[, 1], pc2 = sc[, 2], sx = ctr[1] + pc1 * v1[1], sy = ctr[2] + pc1 * v1[2])
axis_seg <- function(v, len) tibble(x = ctr[1] - len * v[1], y = ctr[2] - len * v[2], xend = ctr[1] + len * v[1], yend = ctr[2] + len * v[2])
report_cor <- cor(report$maths, report$physics)
report_step <- function(k) {
  if (k == 4) {
    return(ggplot(report, aes(pc1, pc2)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = red, linewidth = 1.1) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = navy, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8, colour = grey) +
      coord_fixed(xlim = c(-40, 40), ylim = c(-30, 30)) + theme_slide() +
      labs(x = paste0("PC1: overall mark  (", pct(rp_var[1]), " of the spread)"),
           y = paste0("PC2  (", pct(rp_var[2]), ")"), title = "4 · Turn the page: the same pupils, new axes"))
  }
  p <- ggplot(report, aes(maths, physics)) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(28, 92), ylim = c(26, 90)) + theme_slide() +
    labs(x = "Maths mark", y = "Physics mark",
         title = c("1 · Forty pupils, two marks", "2 · The direction with the most spread: PC1",
                   "3 · Each pupil's shadow on that line: one number")[k])
  if (k >= 2) p <- p + geom_segment(data = axis_seg(v1, 44), aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = red, linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_segment(data = axis_seg(v2, 12), aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = navy, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed")
  if (k == 3) p <- p + geom_segment(aes(xend = sx, yend = sy), colour = grey, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(aes(sx, sy), colour = red, size = 2.2)
  p + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8, colour = grey)
}

# ---- Four subjects: an overall level plus a sciences-against-humanities lean
set.seed(8)
g <- rnorm(200); lean <- rnorm(200, 0, 0.75)
report4 <- tibble(Maths = g + lean + rnorm(200, 0, 0.5), Physics = g + lean + rnorm(200, 0, 0.5),
                  English = g - lean + rnorm(200, 0, 0.5), History = g - lean + rnorm(200, 0, 0.5))
rp4 <- prcomp(report4, scale. = TRUE)
if (sum(rp4$rotation[, 1]) < 0) rp4$rotation[, 1] <- -rp4$rotation[, 1]
if (rp4$rotation["Maths", 2] < 0) rp4$rotation[, 2] <- -rp4$rotation[, 2]
rp4_var <- rp4$sdev^2 / sum(rp4$sdev^2)
stopifnot(all(rp4$rotation[, 1] > 0.4), rp4$rotation["English", 2] < -0.4, rp4$rotation["Physics", 2] > 0.4)
load_style <- list(
  geom_col(alpha = 0.75), coord_flip(),
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Positive" = "#3B4992FF", "Negative" = "#EE0000FF")),
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Loading Value"), theme_minimal(base_size = 15),
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "none"))
report4_loadings <- function(pcs = 1:2) {
  as_tibble(rp4$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "column") |>
    pivot_longer(-column, names_to = "PC", values_to = "value") |>
    mutate(column = factor(column, levels = rev(c("Maths", "Physics", "English", "History"))),
           sign = ifelse(value >= 0, "Positive", "Negative"),
           value = if_else(PC %in% paste0("PC", pcs), value, NA_real_)) |>
    ggplot(aes(column, value, fill = sign)) + facet_wrap(~ PC) + load_style +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.62, 0.62))
}

# ---- The notebook's plots (same code as the student workbook, larger text for the room)
heatmap_plot <- function() {
  train_data |>
    select(starts_with("t")) |>
    cor() |>
    melt(value.name = "correlation") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = correlation)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1), axis.title = element_blank()) +
    labs(title = "IQ Test Correlation Matrix")
}
scree_plot <- function() {
  eigenvalues |>
    ggplot(aes(PC, percent)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(percent, 2)), vjust = -0.3, size = 2.6) +
    labs(title = "Variance Explained by Each PC", y = "Percent Variance") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
cumul_plot <- function() {
  eigenvalues |>
    ggplot(aes(PC, cumulative)) +
    geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(cumulative, 2)), vjust = -0.3, size = 2.6) +
    labs(title = "Cumulative Variance Explained", y = "Cumulative Percent") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
pc_scatter <- function(by_school = FALSE) {
  p <- if (by_school) ggplot(pca_data, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = school)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(navy, red), name = NULL)
       else ggplot(pca_data, aes(PC1, PC2))
  p + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
    labs(title = if (by_school) "The same plot, coloured by school" else "First Two Principal Components") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
loadings_plot <- function() {
  pca_loadings <- pca_fit |>
    tidy(matrix = "loadings") |>
    filter(PC %in% c(1, 2, 3)) |>
    mutate(PC = factor(PC, levels = c("1", "2", "3")), abs_value = abs(value),
           sign = ifelse(value >= 0, "Positive", "Negative"))
  ggplot(pca_loadings, aes(x = reorder(column, abs_value), y = value, fill = sign)) +
    geom_col(alpha = 0.75) +
    facet_wrap(~paste0("PC", PC), scales = "free_y") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Positive" = "#3B4992FF", "Negative" = "#EE0000FF")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Loading Value", fill = "Direction") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")
}

# ---- MCA intuition: what do you watch? Twelve made-up people, four yes/no questions.
yn <- function(x) factor(x, levels = c("n", "y"))
tv <- tribble(~person, ~football, ~f1, ~bakeoff, ~strictly,
  "A", "y", "y", "n", "n",   "B", "y", "y", "n", "n",   "C", "y", "y", "n", "y",   "D", "y", "n", "n", "n",
  "E", "n", "n", "y", "y",   "F", "n", "n", "y", "y",   "G", "n", "y", "y", "y",   "H", "n", "n", "y", "n",
  "I", "y", "y", "y", "y",   "J", "n", "n", "n", "n",   "K", "y", "y", "n", "n",   "L", "n", "n", "y", "y") |>
  mutate(across(-person, yn))
tv_mca <- MCA(as.data.frame(tv[, -1]), graph = FALSE)
tv_pct <- tv_mca$eig[, 2] / 100
tv_coord <- as_tibble(tv_mca$var$coord[, 1:2], rownames = "cat") |>
  rename(d1 = `Dim 1`, d2 = `Dim 2`) |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(str_detect(cat, "football|f1"), "sport", "shows"))
# sport answers and show answers must end up on opposite sides of Dim 1, each "y" opposite its "n"
tv_side <- function(x) sign(tv_coord$d1[tv_coord$cat == x])
stopifnot(tv_side("football_y") == tv_side("f1_y"), tv_side("bakeoff_y") == tv_side("strictly_y"),
          tv_side("football_y") != tv_side("bakeoff_y"), tv_side("football_y") != tv_side("football_n"))
tv_map <- function() {
  ggplot(tv_coord, aes(d1, d2, colour = kind, label = cat)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = grey) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = grey) +
    geom_point(shape = 17, size = 4) +
    geom_text_repel(size = 5.2, show.legend = FALSE, seed = 1, box.padding = 0.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(sport = navy, shows = red), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.25)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.25)) +
    theme_slide() +
    labs(x = paste0("Dim 1 (", pct(tv_pct[1]), ")"), y = paste0("Dim 2 (", pct(tv_pct[2]), ")"),
         title = "The map: one point per answer")
}
tv_rows <- paste0(pmap_chr(tv, function(person, football, f1, bakeoff, strictly) {
  td <- function(x) if (x == "y") '<td class="hl">y</td>' else "<td>n</td>"
  paste0("<tr><td><b>", person, "</b></td>", td(football), td(f1), td(bakeoff), td(strictly), "</tr>")
}), collapse = "\n")
```

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact}
[Data become sparse]{.ct}
Same 30 customers, one more variable, and the neighbourhood empties.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Distance stops meaning much]{.ct}
With 2 variables the farthest customer is `r round(curse_at(2))`× as far as the nearest; with 1,000, `r formatC(curse_at(1000), format = "f", digits = 1)`×. Bad news for kNN.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[And models overfit and slow down]{.ct}
So: **squeeze many variables into a few that keep most of the structure**.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. Last year's income-and-debt example.

- A bank looks for customers similar to the diamond. One variable, income: the diamond has several customers within £6k. Click: add debt, draw the same £6k circle. Fewer are inside. Each variable we add pushes everyone apart.
- Click: the general pattern, simulated with 200 random points. The ratio of the farthest to the nearest neighbour collapses towards 1: "nearest" stops being special. Today's first data set has 24 variables.
- The notebook's callout names three problems: sparse data, overfitting, computation. Last week's models all suffer from at least one.
- The way out works because real variables overlap. Twenty-four ability tests do not measure 24 separate things. That is the next slide.
:::

## The school report: two marks, one number

- Take answers to the question: the average, the sum, "the better one". The average is nearly right; PCA finds it from the data.
- Click: the red line is the direction in which the cloud is longest. The dashed line is what is left over, at a right angle.
- Click: each pupil's position along the red line is their PC1 score. One number instead of two.
- Click: the same points with the red line laid flat. PCA is a rotation: the pupils have not moved relative to each other. The flat direction is where they hardly differ (does a pupil do slightly better in maths or in physics), so dropping it costs little.
- "Variance explained" is the share of the total spread that lies along each new axis.
:::

## Class discussion: two tests that agree

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="on">I · PCA</span><span>II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> line 66 <span>the class discussion before the data</span><i>30 seconds with your neighbour</i></p>
```

::: {.ask}
Two IQ tests are strongly correlated. What would you expect PCA to do with them?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>Delete one of the two tests, since it adds nothing</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>B</b>Give both a similar weight on the same component</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>C</b>Put each on its own component, so they stay apart</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>Nothing: PCA only works on uncorrelated variables</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>B.</b> Maths and physics again: tests that move together share a direction, so one component describes both. PCA keeps every variable and <b>combines</b> them; it never drops a column. Without correlation there would be nothing to compress.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1½ minutes. First item to skip if behind.

- Thirty seconds in pairs, a show of hands, click.
- A is the tempting one: that is feature selection. PCA is feature extraction: new columns built from all the old ones.
- D is backwards: correlation is what PCA feeds on. Uncorrelated variables give components that each explain the same small share.
:::

## Apply PCA: read the recipe

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="on">I · PCA</span><span>II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 99–118 <span>"Apply PCA": the recipe, then <code>bake()</code></span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.anatomy .one}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.52em">pca_recipe &lt;- recipe(school ~ ., data = train_data) |&gt;
  update_role(case, new_role = "ID") |&gt;
  step_zv(all_numeric_predictors()) |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_pca(</span>all_numeric_predictors(),
    <span class="tok">num_comp = 5</span>, keep_original_cols = TRUE) |&gt;
  <span class="tok">prep()</span></p>
```

1. **Same units first.** Otherwise the test with the biggest numbers would be PC1.
2. **The rotation.** Finds the 24 directions, longest first.
3. **Keep five** as new columns `PC1`–`PC5`. We check this choice next.
4. **Do it now**, on the training set. `bake()` then adds the scores.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
pca_data |> select(case, PC1, PC2, PC3)
```

::: {.card .compact .line style="margin-top:0.4em"}
[Read it]{.ct}
Pupil `r pca_data$case[1]` has PC1 = `r formatC(pca_data$PC1[1], format = "f", digits = 1)`: their shadow on the longest direction, well below the average of 0.
:::

::: {.card .compact .dark}
[`school ~ .` is not a model]{.ct}
Nothing is predicted. It only says which columns count as "predictors".
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. Run lines 101–118 together, then read the recipe piece by piece.

- A recipe as in Lab 5, with one new step. `update_role()` keeps `case`, an id, out of the PCA. `step_zv()` drops columns with no variation; there are none here.
- `step_normalize()` matters: PCA looks for spread, and a test scored 0–200 would beat one scored 0–20 only because of its units.
- `prep()` is where the PCA is computed; `bake()` applies it. `keep_original_cols = TRUE` leaves the 24 tests in the table next to the five new columns.
- The next chunk's first line, `pca_recipe$steps[[3]]$res`, reaches into the third step (the PCA) and pulls out the fitted object, so that `tidy()` can give eigenvalues and loadings.
:::

## Answers A: variance explained {.solution}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.9
scree_plot() | cumul_plot()
```

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.3em"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Why five?]{.ct}
PC1 stands out with `r pct(ev(1))`. PC2–PC5 add `r pct(ev(2))`, `r pct(ev(3))`, `r pct(ev(4))`, `r pct(ev(5))`; after that each adds under 4%. No sharp elbow: **a judgement call**.
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[2, 3 and 5 components]{.ct}
`r pct(ev(2, "cumulative"))`, `r pct(ev(3, "cumulative"))` and `r pct(ev(5, "cumulative"))` of the variance. 24 columns became 5 and kept three fifths of the spread.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Why 2 is risky]{.ct}
Two fit on a screen, and show `r pct(ev(2, "cumulative"))`. The other `r pct(1 - ev(2, "cumulative"))` is invisible. Check this number before reading any 2-D plot.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes for this slide, 2 for the next.

- Compare with the school report: there PC1 held over 90%, because two marks were nearly one thing. Twenty-four tests are not one thing: the first component holds under a third.
- There is no rule for the number of components. Common habits: the elbow, a cumulative target (say 60–80%), or cross-validation when the components feed a model.
:::

## Why not PCA?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="on">II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 230–233 <span>the class discussion at the start of Part II</span><i>one minute with your neighbour</i></p>
```

::: {.ask}
Why can't you run PCA on categorical variables? What might "distance" mean instead?
:::

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.6em"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[PCA needs arithmetic]{.ct}
Means, variances, a longest direction. A test score of 60 is 10 above 50. What is **TV − newspaper**? Or the mean of "yes" and "no"?
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Count instead of measure]{.ct}
With categories we can still count **who gave which answers together**. That table of co-occurrences is all MCA uses.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Distance = chosen by different people]{.ct}
Two answers are **close** when mostly the same people give them. Close means "go together", not "similar in value". The notebook calls it chi-square distance.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2 minutes.

- One minute in pairs, then the three cards.
- The lecture's media survey is the example in the first card: news source, age group, voted. No order, no spacing.
- The idea of the map is the same as PCA's: put things on a few axes that keep most of the structure. Only the notion of distance changes.
:::

## What do you watch? A map of answers

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="on">II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{=html}
<table class="mini" style="font-size:0.44em">
<tr><th></th><th>Football</th><th>F1</th><th>Bake Off</th><th>Strictly</th></tr>
`r tv_rows`
</table>

```
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.ask style="font-size:0.75em"}
Which answers tend to come from the same people?
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: false

tv_map()
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Close = same people]{.ct}
`football_y` sits by `f1_y`: the sports fans.
:::
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Opposite = rarely together]{.ct}
Each `_y` faces its own `_n`. Dim 1: sport against shows.

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 5 minutes. The Part II picture to remember; it is the notebook's biplot in miniature.

- Give the room 30 seconds with the table. They will see it: A, B, K watch both sports; E, F, L watch both shows; a few mix.
- Click: MCA on exactly this table. One point per answer (not per person, not per question): 4 questions × 2 answers = 8 points.
- Click: how to read it. Three rules for the lab: (1) close points are answers given by the same people; (2) with two categories, each question's y and n sit on opposite sides, so read one side and you know the other; (3) name an axis by what its two ends have in common, as with loadings.
- The percentages on the axes are the same idea as variance explained.
:::

## Load the data: every answer becomes y or n

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="on">II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 235–252 <span>"Load and prepare ethical norms data"</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.anatomy .one}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.56em">norms &lt;- read_csv("data/wvs-wave-7-ethical-norms.csv") |&gt;
  mutate(<span class="tok">across(everything(),</span>
    ~ as.factor(if_else(<span class="tok">.x &gt; median(.x)</span>, "y", "n"))))

<span class="tok">colnames(norms) &lt;- values</span></p>
```

1. **Every column**: 19 World Values Survey questions, "is this ever justifiable?", from 1 (never) to 10 (always).
2. **Above that question's median: "y".** Otherwise "n". A 10-point scale becomes two categories.
3. **Readable names** instead of `Q177`–`Q195`.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">Share answering "y" <small>after the median split</small></p>
<div class="bars">
  <div><span>premarital sex</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * share_y[["sex_before_marriage"]])`%"></i><b>`r pct(share_y[["sex_before_marriage"]])`</b></div>
  <div><span>divorce</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * share_y[["divorce"]])`%"></i><b>`r pct(share_y[["divorce"]])`</b></div>
  <div><span>stealing property</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * share_y[["stealing_property"]])`%"></i><b>`r pct(share_y[["stealing_property"]])`</b></div>
  <div><span>terrorism</span><i class="hot" style="width:`r round(100 * share_y[["terrorism"]])`%"></i><b>`r pct(share_y[["terrorism"]])`</b></div>
</div>
```

::: {.card .compact .dark style="margin-top:0.6em"}
["y" is not "supports"]{.ct}
For `r n_median1` of the 19 questions the median is 1, "never". There, **y means "anything but never"**: `terrorism_y` is "did not rule it out".
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes. Run lines 237–252 together.

- The notebook says responses run 0–10; the WVS scale is 1 to 10.
- The median split is done per question, so "y" means different things for different questions: for divorce (median `r medians[["Q185"]]`) it means a fairly permissive answer, for stealing it means anything above "never".
- This matters for reading the map: the y-categories of the violence questions are rare answers, and rare categories land far from the middle.
- Note for tutors: `r pct(share_neg, 1)` of the cells are negative codes (−1 don't know, −2 no answer, −5 missing). The notebook's code turns them into "n". It does not change the picture, but it is on the fix list in the lesson plan.
:::

## Apply MCA: one line

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="on">II · MCA</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 254–263 <span>"Apply MCA" and the reflection on the supplementary variable</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.7em">mca &lt;- <span class="tok">MCA(</span><span class="tok">norms</span>, <span class="tok">quali.sup = 1</span>, <span class="tok">graph = FALSE</span>)</p>
```

1. **From `FactoMineR`**, not tidymodels: no recipe, no `prep()`.
2. **A table of factors**: 19 columns of y and n.
3. **Column 1 is supplementary**: `cheating_benefits` is left out when the axes are built.
4. **No automatic plot.** We draw our own next.
:::

::: {.ask style="margin-top:0.5em"}
Why mark a variable as supplementary?
:::

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[It is placed on the map afterwards]{.ct}
The other 18 questions build the axes. `cheating_benefits` is then dropped onto the finished map without shaping it.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[A test of the map]{.ct}
If the map means something, a question it has never seen should land where we expect. A hold-out for a method with no test score.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2½ minutes. Run line 258 together; it takes a couple of seconds on `r big(n_wvs)` rows.

- Compare with Part I: there the PCA sat inside a recipe; here one function call from another package.
- The supplementary variable is the closest thing today to a test set: information kept away from the fit and used to check it.
- Ask for a prediction before the exercise: where should `cheating_benefits_y` land? Near the other dishonesty answers.
:::

::: {.cheat}
[The TV-map rules]{.lbl}

::: {.hints}
- **Close together:** answers given by the same people
- **Opposite sides:** each question's `_y` faces its `_n`: read one side of an axis and you know the other
- **Name an axis** by what its two ends have in common
- **Far from the middle:** a rare answer
:::

```r
fviz_contrib(mca, choice = "var", axes = 1, top = 10)
#   choice = "var"   the answers, not the people
#   axes = 1         for Dim 1 (try axes = 2)
# red dashed line:   an equal share for every answer
```

**Stuck?**

- Start with the right-hand side of Dim 1: are the labels `_y` or `_n`?
- Then compare top right with bottom right

Timing: 4 minutes.

- Dim 1: right against left is y against n for every single question. Someone on the right says "not never" to many things. It is the overall level again.
- Click: Dim 2 splits the y-answers by kind. Top left are the matching "n" answers on private morality; bottom left the "n" answers on violence and dishonesty: the people who rule out harm but not private choices sit towards the bottom.
- Why are `terrorism_y` and `violence_against_spouse_y` so far out? They are rare answers (a quarter of respondents), and rare categories sit far from the middle.
- Click: the supplementary variable lands where predicted.
- Two dimensions show `r pct(sum(mca_pct[1:2]))` of the structure, more than the 41% of the PCA scatter.

Stealing, political violence, social violence, terrorism, bribes, suicide, tax cheating, violence against a spouse. All above the red line (`r formatC(avg_contrib, format = "f", digits = 1)`%, an equal share).

## PCA or MCA?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="done">II · MCA</span><span class="on">Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.small-table}
| | PCA | MCA |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | Numbers with meaningful spacing: test scores, incomes | Categories: yes/no, news source, age group |
| **Built from** | Correlations between variables | Counts of answers given together |
| **Close means** | Similar values | Chosen by the same people |
| **What you read** | Loadings: one bar per variable | The map and contributions: one point per answer |
| **Today** | `step_pca()` in a recipe: 24 tests → 5 components | `MCA()` from `FactoMineR`: 19 questions → 2 dimensions |
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.cards .c2 style="margin-top:0.5em"}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[The same story twice]{.ct}
First axis: a level (overall ability; how much is justifiable). Second: a contrast (verbal against speed; harm against private life).
:::
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Both are linear summaries]{.ct}
Good for seeing structure and for fewer columns in a later model. The naming is always yours.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes. The notebook's last learning objective: compare the two and say when each is appropriate.

- Ask before showing the table: "your survey has age in years, income, and ten yes/no questions. What now?" Either bin the numbers and use MCA, or use a method for mixed data (FAMD, in the same package). The data type decides.
- Click: both labs ended with the same shape of answer. That is common: the first dimension of a battery of similar questions is usually "how much overall".
:::

## Summary

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Why</span><span class="done">I · PCA</span><span class="done">II · MCA</span><span class="on">Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="checks" style="grid-template-columns:1fr">
  <div><b>1</b><span><strong>Why reduce:</strong> with many variables, data are sparse, distances stop telling rows apart, and models overfit. Real variables overlap, so a few new axes can keep most of the structure</span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span><strong>PCA</strong> is the school report: turn the cloud so the first axis runs along its longest direction. Each component has a <strong>share of variance</strong> (how much it keeps) and <strong>loadings</strong> (what it is made of). Same sign: a level. Opposite signs: a contrast. In code: <code>step_normalize()</code>, <code>step_pca()</code>, <code>tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")</code>, <code>tidy(matrix = "loadings")</code></span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span><strong>MCA</strong> is the TV map: one point per answer, close when the same people give them, each y opposite its n. Read the ends of each axis and the <strong>contributions</strong>. In code: <code>MCA()</code>, <code>fviz_mca_biplot()</code>, <code>fviz_contrib()</code></span></div>
</div>
```

**Question:** two components show `r pct(ev(2, "cumulative"))` of the test data. Before you trust a pattern in the PC1–PC2 scatter, what would you check?

::: {.notes}
Wrap-up, 3 minutes.

- Recap in three sentences.
- Exit question: the variance explained, and the same plot for PC3 against PC4; a pattern in two dimensions can vanish or appear once the rest is included.
- Next week: clustering, the other half of unsupervised learning. Today we compressed the columns; next week we group the rows.
:::
